cues.text: Welcome to the Mole Concept.
This recorded Chemistry class uses an AI generated Marin voice.
Begin with what a chemical equation is allowed to change.
In an ordinary chemical reaction, atoms are rearranged; the nuclei are not
converted into different elements.
For a closed system, total mass is conserved to the accuracy of ordinary
chemical measurements.
Gas escaping from an open vessel can make the measured vessel contents lighter
without violating conservation.
The law of definite proportions describes the fixed elemental mass ratio of a
specified pure compound.
Using rounded masses, water has hydrogen to oxygen mass ratio two to sixteen,
or one to eight.
Hydrogen peroxide is a different compound with a different ratio.
The law of multiple proportions compares different compounds formed from the
same two elements: for a fixed mass of one element, the other masses occur in
small whole number ratios.
Carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide illustrate oxygen masses sixteen and thirty
two for carbon mass twelve.
Dalton's model helped explain these laws, but modern atoms have subatomic
structure and isotopes.
Distinguish a useful historical model from its later corrections.
A mole counts specified entities, just as a dozen counts twelve objects.
The Avogadro constant is exactly six point zero two two one four zero seven
six
times ten to the twenty three per mole.
For routine examples we will use six point zero two two times ten to the
twenty
three.
Always name the counted entity: atoms, molecules, ions or formula units.
One mole of oxygen molecules contains two moles of oxygen atoms.
One mole of sodium chloride solid describes formula units in a lattice, not a
collection of separate sodium chloride molecules.
Molar mass connects mass with amount: divide mass by molar mass to obtain
moles.
Using hydrogen one and oxygen sixteen grams per mole, water has molar mass
eighteen grams per mole.
Nine grams of water is therefore half a mole of molecules, or about three
point
zero one one times ten to the twenty three molecules.
That same sample contains one mole of hydrogen atoms and half a mole of oxygen
atoms.
A mole has a fixed entity count, but its mass depends on the substance.
Read every subscript before calculating formula mass.
Parentheses multiply the whole enclosed group.
Calcium hydroxide contains one calcium, two oxygen and two hydrogen atoms per
formula unit.
Using calcium forty, oxygen sixteen and hydrogen one, its formula mass is
forty
plus twice seventeen, or seventy four.
Its molar mass is seventy four grams per mole under those rounded assumptions.
Thus seven point four grams corresponds to zero point one mole of formula
units
and zero point two mole of hydroxide groups.
Counting these groups is not a claim that every solid sample is already
dissolved into free ions.
Percentage composition is the elemental mass contribution divided by total
formula mass, multiplied by one hundred.
For water, oxygen contributes sixteen out of eighteen, about eighty eight
point
nine percent by mass.
A relative molecular mass is dimensionless; the mass of one molecule may be
expressed in atomic mass units, while molar mass has units such as grams per
mole.
These quantities are related but should not be assigned interchangeable units.
Use the atomic masses given in the question.
An empirical formula gives the simplest whole number atom ratio.
A molecular formula gives the actual atom counts in one molecule.
Suppose a compound is forty point zero percent carbon, six point seven percent
hydrogen and fifty three point three percent oxygen by mass.
Assume one hundred grams.
Divide by the rounded atomic molar masses twelve, one and sixteen: the amounts
are approximately three point three three, six point seven and three point
three three moles.
Divide all by the smallest amount to obtain approximately one to two to one.
The empirical formula is C H two O.
Its formula mass is thirty.
If the measured molar mass is one hundred eighty grams per mole, the
multiplier
is six and the molecular formula is C six H twelve O six.
Percentage rounding explains small deviations from ideal integers.
Do not round one point five directly to two: multiply every ratio by two
instead.
Composition alone cannot distinguish all molecular formulas sharing the same
simplest ratio, so additional molar mass information is essential.
Check that the final formula reproduces the approximate percentages.
A balanced equation is a recipe in amounts of substance, not generally in
equal
masses.
Nitrogen plus three hydrogen molecules produces two ammonia molecules.
The same coefficients relate moles.
Start with two moles of nitrogen and three moles of hydrogen.
Divide each available amount by its reactant coefficient: nitrogen gives two,
while hydrogen gives one.
The smaller value identifies hydrogen as limiting.
One mole of nitrogen reacts with three moles of hydrogen, forming two moles of
ammonia and leaving one mole of nitrogen.
Using nitrogen fourteen and hydrogen one grams per mole, the initial masses
are
fifty six grams of nitrogen and six grams of hydrogen.
The products and remainder are thirty four grams of ammonia plus twenty eight
grams of nitrogen, again sixty two grams total.
A limiting reactant is not necessarily the one with the smaller mass or
smaller
raw mole amount.
Convert to moles and compare against the balanced coefficients.
This theoretical result assumes the stated reaction proceeds completely
without
competing chemistry.
Purity changes the amount of reactive material available before the reaction
starts.
Percentage yield compares the actual product obtained with the theoretical
product predicted from that available material.
Keep those two factors separate.
Imagine ten grams of limestone containing eighty percent calcium carbonate by
mass, with inert impurities.
The reactive calcium carbonate mass is eight grams.
On complete thermal decomposition, calcium carbonate gives calcium oxide and
carbon dioxide in a one to one mole ratio.
Using molar masses one hundred for calcium carbonate and forty four for carbon
dioxide, eight grams is zero point zero eight mole and predicts three point
five two grams of carbon dioxide.
If the actual recovered carbon dioxide is two point eight one six grams, the
percentage yield is eighty percent.
The original twenty percent impurity must not be subtracted a second time.
A measured yield above one hundred percent usually signals wet or impure
product, a mistaken assumption or measurement error, rather than creation of
extra matter.
State whether impurities react before treating them as inert.
For an ideal gas, pressure times volume equals amount times the gas constant
times absolute temperature.
Gas volume is therefore not a universal measure of moles unless temperature
and
pressure are specified.
At two hundred seventy three point one five kelvin and one atmosphere, one
mole
of ideal gas occupies about twenty two point four one litres.
At the same temperature and one bar, the value is about twenty two point seven
one litres.
Do not silently interchange these conventions.
Equal gas volumes at equal temperature and pressure contain equal amounts in
the ideal gas approximation.
For solutions, molarity is solute moles divided by solution volume in litres.
Zero point two zero mole in five hundred millilitres of solution gives zero
point four zero mole per litre.
During dilution without reaction or loss, solute amount stays constant, so
initial concentration times initial volume equals final concentration times
final volume.
Taking fifty millilitres of this solution and diluting to two hundred
millilitres gives zero point one zero mole per litre.
Use final solution volume, not merely the volume of water added.
A reliable mixed problem follows a chain of quantities with units attached.
Suppose five grams of a sample contains eighty percent magnesium by mass and
inert material.
Excess acid reacts with magnesium to give magnesium ions and hydrogen gas, one
mole of hydrogen per mole of magnesium.
With magnesium molar mass twenty four grams per mole, the reactive mass is
four
grams and the amount is one sixth of a mole.
At the stated ideal gas molar volume of twenty four litres per mole, complete
reaction predicts four litres of hydrogen.
If only seventy five percent of that theoretical gas is recovered, the
collected volume is three litres at those same conditions.
The acid is explicitly in excess; otherwise its amount would also need
checking.
Do not multiply by a percentage twice or apply a mass ratio directly as a mole
ratio.
Keep extra digits during calculation and round at the end according to the
supplied measurements.
Exact coefficients and entity definitions do not limit significant figures.
Use the practice questions to check each conversion before attempting longer
reaction chains.
